# The Vision:

To build a predictive application that enables the Commissioner’s Office to estimate property values and, more importantly, explain why those prices are shifting.

## Strategy {.center}

-   CPI Adjustment: Normalize historical sales to today's dollar.
-   Market Segmentation: Use "Market Type" (Single-Family vs. Multi-Family) as interaction terms—recognizing that an extra bedroom in a condo adds different value than an extra bedroom on a ranch.
-   The Application: An interactive application that will output pricing predictions and add transparency in the valuation process.

# Methodology

## Phase 1: {.center}

Feature Drivers: Identify the drivers of what makes properties different. 
These drivers are found in my PCA. Drivers that have been found will be discussed later on.

## Phase 2: {.center}

Price Sub-Markets: Identify the sub-markets within housing markets (housing markets: single family, multi-family, etc.) These sub-markets are found in Ryan and Lucca's UMAPS.

## Phase 3: {.center}

Price Prediction: Utilize findings from feature extraction and sub-market classifications to then predict housing prices, adjusting for CPI in the process. The goal of these models is to capture 90% or more of the variation in price. These predictions are currently being curated!

```{python}
#| label: function creation
#| include: false

def normalize(df):
    """
    Returns two dataframes:
    1. df_quantile: Everything forced to normal via Quantile Transformation.
    2. df_comp: Each column transformed by the 'winner' of YJ vs. Quantile.
    """
    df_quantile = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    df_comp = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    
    numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
    
    for col in numeric_cols:
        data_raw = df[col].values.reshape(-1, 1)

        # Yeo-Johnson
        yj_data, lmbda = stats.yeojohnson(df[col])
        _, yj_p = stats.normaltest(yj_data)
        
        # Normality test for the Quantile data
        qt_engine = QuantileTransformer(output_distribution='normal', 
                                        n_quantiles=min(len(df), 1000), 
                                        random_state=42)
        qt_data = qt_engine.fit_transform(data_raw).flatten()
        _, qt_p = stats.normaltest(qt_data)
        
        if yj_p >= qt_p:
            # Determine suffix for YJ winner
            if -0.1 <= lmbda <= 0.1: suffix = "log"
            elif 0.4 <= lmbda <= 0.6: suffix = "sqrt"
            elif 0.9 <= lmbda <= 1.1: suffix = "linear"
            elif lmbda < 0: suffix = "inv"
            else: suffix = "pow"
            df_comp[f"{col}_{suffix}"] = yj_data
        else:
            df_comp[f"{col}_quant"] = qt_data
            
    print(f"Experiments complete for {len(numeric_cols)} variables.")
    return df_comp

```

# Current Insights (Phase 1)

## Insights: "The Standard vs. The Luxury" {.center}

Finding: Only 30% of property variation is driven by "Standard Features" (Bed/Bath/Sqft).

The "So What?": 70% of what makes properties in Iron County unique comes from "Luxury" or "Nuance" features (sheds, pools, etc.). Interesting feature fact: Half Baths act like a "luxury" feature in the data.

Actionable Step: Our model cannot just look at the basics; we must include these "luxury" indicators to reach our 90% accuracy goal.

PCA Components: - PC1: contains standard variables.\
- PC2: focus on recreational outdoor features (ex pools, rec courts, etc)\
- PC3: focus on utility outdoor features (ex sheds, barns, etc)\
- PC4: focus on aggrecultural vs recreational utility features (carport v barn)\
- PC5: focus on guest features vs personal features (guest house v gazebo)\
- PC6: focus on niche\
- PC7: focus on niche\
- PC8: focus on niche\
- PC9: focus on external vehical storage vs general utility (detached garage v shed)\
- PC10: focus on attached vehical storage vs general utility (carport v shed)\
- PC11: focus on basement space and completion over vehical storage\
- PC12: focus on the land\
- PC13: focus on half-bath\

```{python}
#| label: identify number of clusters
#| include: false

inertia = []
k_range = range(1, 11) 

for k in k_range:
    kmeans_test = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init="auto")
    kmeans_test.fit(pca_df)
    inertia.append(kmeans_test.inertia_)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(k_range, inertia, marker='o', linestyle='--')
plt.title('Elbow Method to Identify Optimal Clusters')
plt.xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)')
plt.ylabel('Inertia (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares)')
plt.xticks(k_range)
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()

```

```{python}
#| label: final clustering
#| include: false

optimal_k = 13

final_model = KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, random_state=42, n_init="auto")
labels = final_model.fit_predict(umap_embeddings)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7))
plt.scatter(umap_embeddings[:, 0], umap_embeddings[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='viridis', s=5)
plt.colorbar(label='Cluster Label')
plt.title(f"UMAP Projection with {optimal_k} K-Means Clusters")
plt.show()

```

```{python}
#| label: HDBSCAN Clustering
#| include: false

for i in range(100,600,100):
    print(f"HDBSCAN with min_cluster_size = {i}")
    clusterer = hdbscan.HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=i, gen_min_span_tree=True)
    cluster_labels = clusterer.fit_predict(umap_embeddings)

    n_clusters = len(set(cluster_labels)) - (1 if -1 in cluster_labels else 0)

    score = validity.validity_index(umap_embeddings.astype('double'), cluster_labels)
    print(f"DBCV Score: {score:.3f}")

    plt.title(f"UMAP Projection with {n_clusters} HDBSCAN Clusters")
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
    plt.scatter(
        umap_embeddings[:, 0], 
        umap_embeddings[:, 1], 
        c=cluster_labels,      
        cmap='Spectral', 
        s=5)
    plt.title('Housing Clusters via HDBSCAN (Organic Shapes)')
    plt.colorbar(label='Cluster Label')
    plt.title(f"UMAP Projection with {n_clusters} HDBSCAN Clusters")
    plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: cpi adjustment
#| include: false

cpi.update()

merged_df['SaleYear'] = pd.to_datetime(merged_df['ReviewedDate'], unit='D', origin='1899-12-30').dt.year

unique_years = [int(y) for y in merged_df['SaleYear'].unique() if pd.notna(y)]
cpi_lookup = {}
for year in unique_years:
    try:
        cpi_lookup[year] = cpi.get(year)
    except Exception:
        cpi_lookup[year] = cpi.get(2024)
target_cpi = cpi.get(2024)

merged_df['cpi_index_at_sale'] = merged_df['SaleYear'].map(cpi_lookup)
merged_df['CPI Adjusted Sold Price'] = (merged_df['Sold Price'] * target_cpi) / merged_df['cpi_index_at_sale']

merged_df[['Sold Price', 'CPI Adjusted Sold Price']].describe()

```

# Road Map & Next Steps

## CPI Adjustments {.center}

Reasoning: Due to inflation, the value of a dollar today is not the same as it was a year ago or will be in a year. To ensure that all of the dollar amounts we are predicting equate to the same value, we need to adjust for these market fluxuations.

Role of the Students: Our role is to prepare the data for the adjustments by consolidating insights about markets and sub-markets in with a master dataset for the Commissioners office to work with.

Role of the Commissioner Office: The role of the commissioner office is to conduct the CPI adjustments on the master dataset and return it back to the students for model integration.

## Modeling {.center}

Modeling: As we move into the modeling, we want to combine insights from the unsupervised modeling into our supervised modeling process. As mentioned previously, we will want to add interaction variables for markets and sub-markets. Another interaction variable that may be beneficial is location, as rural areas may be priced differently compared to urban areas. As previously mentioned, the goal of the modeling is to account for 90% or more of the variation in price.

Validation: As we model, we need to validate the models so that the predictions can be trusted.

## Application {.center}

Deployment: Once a model is chosen, it will then be implemented into a user-friendly platform for the Commissioners Office, such that predictions and drivers are identified.

```{python}
    'PC1', 'PC2', 'PC3', 'PC4', 'PC5', 'PC6', 'PC7', 'PC8', 'PC9', 'PC10', 'PC11', 'PC12', 'PC13', 'PC14' ,'PC15', 'PC16', 'PC17', 'PC18', 'PC19', 'PC20']]
y = pcadata['CPI Adjusted Sold Price']
mask = y.notna()
X, y = X[mask], y[mask]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=2026)

X_with_const = sm.add_constant(X_train)
sm_model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_with_const).fit()

print(sm_model.summary())

vif_data = pd.DataFrame()
vif_data["feature"] = X_with_const.columns
vif_data["VIF"] = [variance_inflation_factor(X_with_const.values, i) 
                   for i in range(len(X_with_const.columns))]

print(vif_data.sort_values(by="VIF", ascending=False))

```

```{python}
#| label: random forest on primary components

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

pcadata = pcadata[pcadata['CPI Adjusted Sold Price'] != 0]

pc_cols = [f'PC{i}' for i in range(1, 21)]

# 2. Create a temporary combined dataframe to ensure perfect row alignment
temp_df = pcadata[pc_cols + ['CPI Adjusted Sold Price']].dropna()

# 3. Separate them back out
X = temp_df[pc_cols]
y = temp_df['CPI Adjusted Sold Price']

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=2026)

rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, random_state=2026)
rf_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = rf_model.predict(X_test)

print(f"R^2 Score: {r2_score(y_test, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"Mean Absolute Error: ${mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred):,.2f}")

importances = pd.Series(rf_model.feature_importances_, index=X.columns)
importances.sort_values().plot(kind='barh', title='Importance of Principal Components')
```

```{python}
#| label: optimized random forest

from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
import numpy as np

valid_data = pcadata[pcadata['CPI Adjusted Sold Price'] > 0].copy()

# 2. Create your target (Sqrt transform)
valid_data['target'] = np.sqrt(valid_data['CPI Adjusted Sold Price'])

# 3. Define X and y from the SAME dataframe
pc_cols = [f'PC{i}' for i in range(1, 21)]
X = valid_data[pc_cols]
y = valid_data['target']

# Now they are guaranteed to have the same number of rows
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=2026)

param_dist = {
    'n_estimators': [100, 200, 500],           # Number of trees (more is usually better, but slower)
    'max_depth': [10, 20, 30, None],          # How deep each tree goes (prevents overfitting)
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10],          # Min samples required to split a node
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 2, 4],            # Min samples required at a leaf node
    'max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', None]    # Number of features to consider at each split
}

rf_random = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=RandomForestRegressor(random_state=2026),
    param_distributions=param_dist,
    n_iter=20, 
    cv=5, 
    scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error', 
    verbose=2, 
    random_state=2026, 
    n_jobs=-1 
)

rf_random.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Best Parameters: {rf_random.best_params_}")

# 5. Use the best model for predictions
best_rf = rf_random.best_estimator_
y_pred_tuned = best_rf.predict(X_test)

```

```{python}
#| label: random forest model validation take 5
#| include: false

# 1. Filter out the extreme outliers from your test sets
# 1. Identify and remove outliers from the TRAINING set (where the model learns)
y_train_pred_initial = rf_model.predict(X_train) 
train_residuals = y_train - y_train_pred_initial
std_train_residuals = (train_residuals - train_residuals.mean()) / train_residuals.std()

# Create mask for training (keeping only those <= 5 std devs)
train_clean_mask = std_train_residuals.abs() <= 5
X_train_clean = X_train[train_clean_mask]
y_train_clean = y_train[train_clean_mask]

# 2. Use your existing mask for the TEST set
X_test_clean = X_test[~extreme_outlier_mask]
y_test_clean = y_test[~extreme_outlier_mask]

# 3. RE-FIT the model on the CLEAN training data
rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, min_samples_split=2, min_samples_leaf=2, max_depth=None, random_state=2026)
rf_model.fit(X_train_clean, y_train_clean)

# 4. Predict on the CLEAN test set
y_pred_clean = rf_model.predict(X_test_clean)

# 5. Report new metrics
print(f"New R^2 Score: {r2_score(y_test_clean, y_pred_clean):.4f}")
print(f"New Mean Absolute Error: ${mean_absolute_error(y_test_clean, y_pred_clean):,.2f}")

# 6. Plot updated feature importance
importances = pd.Series(rf_model.feature_importances_, index=X.columns)
importances.sort_values().plot(kind='barh', title='Importance of Principal Components (Cleaned Data)')

```
